result:
There's a particular pleasure in noticing things that have no practical use. I mean things like the way "scintillating" sounds exactly like what it describes, or how certain numbers feel personality-laden even though that's obviously absurd—seven feels different from eight in some way that has nothing to do with mathematics and everything to do with some accident of how we learned to count on our fingers, or how those numerals look, or some folk association nobody can quite trace. This kind of noticing doesn't get you anywhere. It doesn't solve problems. But I think it might be one of the realest forms of attention there is, because it's attention without an agenda. You're not looking at the thing because you need something from it. You're just looking.

I want to spend some time on this idea of looking without needing, because I think it's underrated, and because most of the structures we build for ourselves—schools, jobs, even hobbies once they calcify into identities—train us out of it. You learn to look at a forest and see board feet of lumber, or carbon sequestration, or a nice backdrop for a photo. All useful ways of seeing. But there's a way of looking at a forest where you're not extracting anything, where the forest is just astonishingly there, doing its slow combustion of sunlight into wood, completely indifferent to your categories. Children do this naturally and then get talked out of it by well-meaning adults who ask "what is it" until the kid learns that the correct response to wonder is classification.

I don't think classification is the enemy, to be clear. Knowing the name of a bird doesn't ruin the bird. Richard Feynman made this point well once, in response to someone who suggested that scientific knowledge drains the beauty out of things—he said something like, knowing the inner workings of a flower doesn't subtract from its beauty, it adds a whole structure of beauty invisible to someone who only sees the surface. I think that's right. But there's a difference between knowledge that opens more doors and knowledge that closes the original door behind you. The trick, if there is one, is holding both: the bird's name and the simple fact of the bird, irreducible, doing its bird things regardless of what you call it.

This makes me think about the strange status of language generally—how much weight we put on getting the right word, as though words were containers that could fully hold their referents, when actually they're more like gestures, rough pointings-at. You say "I'm exhausted" and the word does almost nothing to convey the specific flavor of exhaustion you mean—is it the bone-tired of physical labor, or the static-fuzz exhaustion of decision fatigue, or the hollow exhaustion of grief, which barely feels like tiredness at all and more like the body's systems running at half-voltage. English has one word for all of these and so we layer on intonation, context, facial expression, repetition ("I'm exhausted, I'm so exhausted") trying to triangulate toward the specific thing. Other languages carve the territory differently and presumably have their own blind spots and their own unexpectedly precise tools. I've always liked the fact that there's no perfect language, no one-to-one mapping between word and world, because it means communication is always a kind of faith. You say something and trust that it'll land close enough. Most of the time it does. The cases where it doesn't—where someone hears something completely different from what you meant—are usually more revealing than the successful cases, because they show you the seams, the places where your private vocabulary and someone else's don't quite overlap.

I keep circling back to the idea of seams, actually, because I think a lot of what's interesting is at the edges of things rather than in their centers. The center of most categories is boring—everyone agrees a robin is a bird, nobody loses sleep over it. It's the edges that are interesting: is a virus alive? Is a building a single object or a million tiny objects glued together? At what point does a heap of sand stop being a heap? These aren't just word games, even though they look like word games. They're places where our categories, which we built for everyday convenience, turn out not to carve reality cleanly, and we get to watch the carving fail in real time. I find a real, almost physical pleasure in this kind of failure. It's like watching a magic trick and being shown the wires. The categories were never reality itself, just useful fictions, and every edge case is a small, harmless reminder of that.

This is maybe why I like puzzles and games more than I like most forms of so-called productive work, if I'm honest. A puzzle has the rare property of being a system whose rules you fully understand. You know exactly what the boundaries are, exactly what counts as a solution. The world almost never offers you that. Most real problems—how to be a good friend, what to do with your life, how to fix a relationship that's gone quietly wrong—have no fixed rules and no clear win condition. The relief of a crossword puzzle, or a chess problem, or a Rubik's Cube, is the relief of operating inside a tiny, fully specified universe where effort and understanding actually produce results you can verify. I don't think this is escapism exactly, or not only that. I think it's more like a vacation for the part of your brain that's exhausted from operating under uncertainty all the time, a place where it can stretch out and solve something completely, instead of muddling through something partially, which is what real life mostly requires.

But then again, muddling has its own pleasures, which I don't want to undersell. There's a kind of muddling that's just bad—aimless, anxious, the kind where you're muddling because you're avoiding clarity that's actually available to you if you'd just sit still and think. But there's another kind of muddling that's more like improvisation, like jazz, where you genuinely don't know what the right move is, and you make one anyway, provisionally, ready to revise. This is most of what being a person actually consists of, moment to moment. We talk about decisions as though they're discrete events—you weigh the options, you choose—but most of what we do is more like leaning. You lean toward the thing that seems slightly better, not because you've resolved all uncertainty but because you have to move and standing still isn't actually neutral, it's its own choice with its own costs. I think a lot of anxiety comes from mistaking the leaning for something that should feel like the certainty of a solved puzzle. People beat themselves up for not being sure, as though sureness were the normal condition and its absence a personal failing, when actually unsureness is just the baseline hum of being a finite creature making decisions with incomplete information about a world that won't sit still long enough to be fully known.

I want to say something about time here, because I think time is the thing that makes muddling necessary in the first place. If you had infinite time you could afford total certainty—you could gather all the information, run all the experiments, wait out all the uncertainty. But you don't have infinite time, you have this time, this stretch of however many decades, ticking down whether you act or not, and so every decision is really a bet made under a deadline, even when the deadline isn't explicit. I find this both terrifying and, weirdly, calming. Terrifying for the obvious reason. Calming because it means perfectionism is not just emotionally costly but actually irrational—if there's no way to wait for full information, then waiting for it is its own kind of failure, dressed up as caution. At some point "I want to be sure before I act" quietly becomes "I am choosing not to act," and the choosing gets to hide behind the wanting, as though it weren't a choice at all.

I notice I've drifted from forests and birds to time and decision-making, which is maybe just what happens when you write without a destination—you start somewhere concrete and end up somewhere abstract, pulled along by whatever association feels most alive at each step. I don't think this is a flaw in the writing, though I can see how it might read like one if you wanted an argument with a thesis and supporting points marching in formation. I'm more interested, today, in writing the way thinking actually happens, which is associative and looping and occasionally doubles back on itself to pick up a thread it dropped three paragraphs ago.

So let me pick up the thread about looking without needing, because I don't think I finished with it. I said it's a kind of attention without an agenda, and I want to push on that a little, because I'm not sure total agenda-lessness is even possible, or desirable. Even the most contemplative attention has some shape to it—you're not looking at everything at once, you're looking at this leaf, this sentence, this particular shaft of light on the particular afternoon, and the choosing of where to look is itself a kind of agenda, however soft. Maybe what I actually mean isn't agenda-less attention but attention that isn't trying to extract a verdict. You can look at a leaf and just notice its asymmetry, the way one side curls slightly more than the other, without needing that noticing to resolve into "this is a healthy leaf" or "this is an interesting case of fluctuating asymmetry I could write a paper about." The noticing can just stay noticing. It doesn't have to graduate into knowledge or action.

This connects, weirdly, to something I think about with conversation—the difference between talking in order to arrive somewhere and talking as a way of being somewhere. A lot of conversation, especially among people trying to be efficient or impressive, is really just a sequence of small negotiations toward a destination: I say this to get you to agree, you say that to correct my premise, eventually we land on a shared conclusion or we don't and someone wins by default. That kind of talk has its place. But the best conversations I can remember weren't like that at all—they were more like two people taking a walk with no itinerary, commenting on whatever passed, occasionally surprised by where the path went, neither one trying to get the other anywhere. Those conversations are rare because they require both people to give up, temporarily, the desire to be right or useful or persuasive, which is a surprisingly hard thing to give up, harder than it sounds, because being right feels like safety and safety is addictive.

I think a lot of what's wrong with public discourse, the big capital-D Discourse that everyone complains about, is that it's almost entirely the first kind of talk and almost none of the second. Everyone's trying to arrive somewhere, trying to win, trying to extract a concession or a confession, and there's no room left for the kind of talk that's just walking together commenting on the scenery. Even disagreement can be like that, actually—you can disagree with someone the way you'd point out a different bird than the one your walking companion just noticed, without it being a referendum on who's the better birdwatcher. But that requires a kind of safety that's in short supply, because so much of public talk happens between people who don't trust each other, who reasonably suspect that any admission of uncertainty will be used against them. So everyone over-asserts, and the over-asserting calcifies into positions, and the positions calcify into identities, and pretty soon nobody can update on anything because updating would mean admitting the identity was provisional all along, which feels like a kind of death.

I don't have a solution to this, and I'm suspicious of anyone who claims to. But I do think there's something to be said for practicing, in small low-stakes contexts, the kind of talk that doesn't need to arrive anywhere—not because it'll fix the big discourse problems, but because it might keep some part of you limber, some capacity for genuine curiosity about another person's view that doesn't immediately collapse into strategy. I think of it like stretching. You don't stretch in the middle of the race. You stretch beforehand, in private, when nothing's at stake, so that the muscle is ready when something actually is at stake.

I started this with birds and forests and I want to end somewhere that at least gestures back at that, because I think there's a thread connecting all of this—the noticing without needing, the comfort of puzzles versus the necessity of muddling, the conversations that walk rather than arrive—and the thread is something like: most of what's valuable doesn't announce itself as valuable. It doesn't come with a verdict attached. The forest doesn't tell you whether to see it as lumber or as a miracle of slow-motion combustion; the conversation doesn't tell you whether it was productive; the leaf doesn't resolve into a lesson. The verdicts are things we add, usually because we've been trained to need them, to need every experience to cash out into something portable—a lesson, a takeaway, a piece of content. And I don't think there's anything wrong with takeaways exactly. But I think the richest part of being alive, if I had to bet on it, is in the noticing that happens before the takeaway gets extracted, in that brief window where the thing is just itself, unprocessed, not yet flattened into use. It's a small window, easy to miss, easy to rush past on the way to the verdict. But it's there, available, almost always, if you're willing to look without immediately asking what the looking is for.
